title: Identify implementation, side-channel, timing, and fault-injection paths: concept decisions 1
teachingQuestion: What can this attacker observe or induce around the computation, and which defense fits that path?
focalInsight: Observation, access, repeatability, error behavior, hardware, and physical interfaces define implementation risk.
caption: Read across a row to connect meaning, decision and consequence. Use the retrieval answer to check your explanation after reading the linked scenario.

nodes.label: Implementation Attack
nodes.definition: Attack against behavior around a computation rather than the mathematical design itself.
nodes.detail: Attack against behavior around a computation rather than the mathematical design itself.
nodes.decision: Model remote, local, co-resident, maintainer, supply-chain, and physical access.
nodes.failureExample: A system selects a sound algorithm but leaks a key in debug output.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Implementation behavior belongs in the threat model.

nodes.label: Side Channel
nodes.definition: Leakage via timing, power, electromagnetic signals, cache behavior, or errors.
nodes.detail: Leakage via timing, power, electromagnetic signals, cache behavior, or errors.
nodes.decision: Assess measurable signal, attacker access, repeatability, and secret exposure.
nodes.failureExample: A co-resident workload observes cache patterns during key operations.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: A side channel reveals behavior without reading the key directly.

nodes.label: Timing Attack
nodes.decision: Use constant-time comparison or equivalent where timing is observable and sensitive.
nodes.failureExample: An authentication check returns faster on the first mismatched byte.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Time differences can disclose secret progress.

nodes.label: Fault Injection
nodes.definition: Inducing voltage, clock, memory, input, or environmental faults to alter execution.
nodes.detail: Inducing voltage, clock, memory, input, or environmental faults to alter execution.
nodes.decision: Use integrity checks, redundancy, protected boot/update, tamper measures, and physical controls as justified.
nodes.failureExample: A fault makes a device skip secure-boot verification.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Fault resistance requires a response to abnormal execution.

nodes.label: Error Handling
nodes.definition: Design of failure responses so errors do not reveal secrets or permit unsafe continuation.
nodes.detail: Design of failure responses so errors do not reveal secrets or permit unsafe continuation.
nodes.decision: Normalize external errors, log protected detail, and fail securely.
nodes.failureExample: Different login errors reveal whether an account, password, or token was valid.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Useful operator evidence need not be useful attacker feedback.

nodes.label: Constant Time
nodes.definition: Implementation approach that avoids secret-dependent timing where needed.
nodes.detail: Implementation approach that avoids secret-dependent timing where needed.
nodes.decision: Use for operations and comparisons exposed to an attacker’s timing measurements.
nodes.failureExample: A compiler optimization reintroduces secret-dependent branch timing.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Constant-time needs assurance after code and toolchain changes.

nodes.label: Hardware Security
nodes.definition: Use of hardware or service boundaries to protect secrets and sensitive operations.
nodes.detail: Use of hardware or service boundaries to protect secrets and sensitive operations.
nodes.decision: Choose when extraction resistance, controlled operations, and physical assurance matter.
nodes.failureExample: A hardware-backed key is accessible through an enabled debug interface.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Hardware protection depends on configuration and interface control.

nodes.label: Physical Security
nodes.definition: Controls limiting physical observation, tampering, maintenance abuse, and device theft.
nodes.detail: Controls limiting physical observation, tampering, maintenance abuse, and device theft.
nodes.decision: Apply by facility, device exposure, attacker capability, and consequence.
nodes.failureExample: An unattended device exposes test pads and diagnostic ports.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Physical access can change the attacker model completely.

nodes.label: Secure Coding
nodes.definition: Engineering practice that avoids unsafe input, state, memory, error, and dependency behavior.
nodes.detail: Engineering practice that avoids unsafe input, state, memory, error, and dependency behavior.
nodes.decision: Use vetted libraries, review, tests, patching, and controlled changes.
nodes.failureExample: A parser flaw lets malformed input bypass protocol validation.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Secure crypto requires secure surrounding code.
